brief.constraints:

Observed: The design also shows a single filled CTA, 'Start free trial' (184x52px), with a quiet 'See how it works' text link beneath it. The headline is one 7-word sentence.

Observed: The subhead is a 44-word paragraph set at 13px with a 640px measure, producing lines of roughly 105-115 characters.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the hero section of a direct-to-consumer skincare store (marketing landing page) for first-time shoppers on mobile on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [STRENGTH] One dominant action plus one quiet alternative is exactly the hierarchy discipline working: the eye lands on the primary without deliberation, and the secondary does not compete. The 7-word headline is a single idea the visitor can hold. Principle at stake: One idea per screen, one primary action; restraint is the design.

Step 2 - Typography. [STRENGTH] 21 words at 18px over a ~65-character measure is a comfortable reading task; the hierarchy is carried by size and weight alone, with no color or decoration needed. Type is doing the work decoration wants to do. Principle at stake: Comfortable line length and size; typography as the primary design tool. [MINOR] 13px is below the comfortable body floor for desktop marketing copy, and 105+ character lines force a long, error-prone eye return on every line. The type is asking the reader to work before the product has earned any attention. Principle at stake: Line length and body size serve the reader's eye; long lines make the return trip tiring.
output:
Ranked findings (most severe first):
1. [MINOR] hero section - The 44-word subhead runs at 13px across a 640px measure, yielding ~105-115 characters per line. That is roughly double a comfortable reading measure at a size that already strains. Principle: Line length and body size serve the reader's eye; long lines make the return trip tiring [chunks: 1s-practical-typography#3, 1s-material-3#5]. Suggested fix: Reset the subhead to 17-18px, cap the measure near 560px (about 60-70 characters), and cut the copy to under 25 words. One idea, one breath. (proposed, not applied)

- CONFIRM: the 21-word subhead at 18px / 560px measure / 1.55 line-height reads comfortably in one glance and needs no decorative support. Disciplined type carrying the hierarchy. reasoning_trace:

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] Three equally loud buttons is a hierarchy failure before it is a copy problem: the eye has no primary to land on, so the visitor must read and compare all three before knowing which is safe. That comparison is the designer's job being pushed onto the user. Principle at stake: One primary action per screen; competing primaries force the user to do the designer's job. [MAJOR] When text needs a scrim to survive, the video is the problem, not the text. The partial scrim means legibility varies line by line, and the screen fails the grayscale test: strip color and the subhead dissolves into the footage. Principle at stake: Clarity: controls and text must be unmistakable; legibility beats atmosphere; the grayscale test. [STRENGTH] One dominant action plus one quiet alternative is exactly the hierarchy discipline working: the eye lands on the primary without deliberation, and the secondary does not compete. The 7-word headline is a single idea the visitor can hold. Principle at stake: One idea per screen, one primary action; restraint is the design.

Step 2 - Typography. [MINOR] 13px is below the comfortable body floor for desktop marketing copy, and 105+ character lines force a long, error-prone eye return on every line. The type is asking the reader to work before the product has earned any attention. Principle at stake: Line length and body size serve the reader's eye; long lines make the return trip tiring. [MINOR] Body spacing applied to display type makes the headline read as scattered large letters instead of one visual unit; at 56px the whitespace inside and between letters dominates. This is an optical error, not a taste error. Principle at stake: Display type needs tighter spacing than body; judge headlines as shapes at their actual size.

Step 4 - Motion. [MINOR] The motion explains none of the five acceptable things: it gives no feedback, shows no origin, preserves no continuity, directs no focus, bridges no spatial change. It is theater spending the user's attention and bandwidth, and it ignores the reduced-motion preference entirely. Principle at stake: Every animation must explain something (feedback, origin, continuity, focus, spatial change); stillness is the default.

Atmosphere is taxing legibility. Principle: Clarity: controls and text must be unmistakable; legibility beats atmosphere; the grayscale test [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#1, 1s-refactoring-ui#5, 1s-apple-hig#11]. Suggested fix: Either commit to a full-bleed scrim (60-70% gradient across the whole text block) or replace the video with a still frame dimmed to a consistent tone. 3. [MINOR] hero section - The 44-word subhead runs at 13px across a 640px measure, yielding ~105-115 characters per line. 4. Principle: Display type needs tighter spacing than body; judge headlines as shapes at their actual size [chunks: 1s-practical-typography#6]. Suggested fix: Set display type by eye at its actual size: tighten line-height toward 1.05-1.15 and apply slight negative tracking until the headline reads as a single shape. (proposed, not applied)
5. [MINOR] hero section - A 12-second looping video autoplays behind the hero with no pause control and no reduced-motion alternative. The motion explains nothing about the product or the user's position; it is decoration with a bandwidth cost. Principle: Every animation must explain something (feedback, origin, continuity, focus, spatial change); stillness is the default [chunks: 1s-emil-kowalski#1, 1s-emil-kowalski#2]. Suggested fix: Default to a still frame; play motion only on user request. Honor the OS reduced-motion setting with an instant static frame, and never make the value proposition depend on a moving background. (proposed, not applied)

This is the one-action-per-screen discipline applied correctly. Why it works: One idea per screen, one primary action; restraint is the design [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#1, 1s-refactoring-ui#7].

Region under review: hero section (marketing landing page, desktop web (1440px)).
The hero of a regional real-estate listings site: a full-viewport section with a looping background video of a team at work, a two-line display headline, a paragraph subhead, and call-to-action buttons.
Observed: Three buttons sit side by side under the subhead: 'Start free trial', 'Book a demo', and 'Watch the film'. All three are the same size (160x48px), the same filled style, and the same brand-blue background.
Observed: The headline is white 56px type set directly over the looping background video. A 40% black gradient scrim sits only behind the top third of the text block; the subhead's lower lines sit over a bright window in the footage.
Observed: The subhead is a 44-word paragraph set at 13px with a 640px measure, producing lines of roughly 105-115 characters.
Observed: The 56px display headline uses the same 1.6 line-height and default letter-spacing as the 16px body style.
Observed: The background video autoplays on load, loops every 12 seconds, and has no pause control. No reduced-motion variant is provided.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the hero section of a regional real-estate listings site (marketing landing page) for buyers browsing homes on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] Three equally loud buttons is a hierarchy failure before it is a copy problem: the eye has no primary to land on, so the visitor must read and compare all three before knowing which is safe. That comparison is the designer's job being pushed onto the user. Principle at stake: One primary action per screen; competing primaries force the user to do the designer's job. [MAJOR] When text needs a scrim to survive, the video is the problem, not the text. The partial scrim means legibility varies line by line, and the screen fails the grayscale test: strip color and the subhead dissolves into the footage. Principle at stake: Clarity: controls and text must be unmistakable; legibility beats atmosphere; the grayscale test.

Step 2 - Typography. [MINOR] 13px is below the comfortable body floor for desktop marketing copy, and 105+ character lines force a long, error-prone eye return on every line. The type is asking the reader to work before the product has earned any attention. Principle at stake: Line length and body size serve the reader's eye; long lines make the return trip tiring. [MINOR] Body spacing applied to display type makes the headline read as scattered large letters instead of one visual unit; at 56px the whitespace inside and between letters dominates. This is an optical error, not a taste error. Principle at stake: Display type needs tighter spacing than body; judge headlines as shapes at their actual size.

Step 4 - Motion. [MINOR] The motion explains none of the five acceptable things: it gives no feedback, shows no origin, preserves no continuity, directs no focus, bridges no spatial change. It is theater spending the user's attention and bandwidth, and it ignores the reduced-motion preference entirely. Principle at stake: Every animation must explain something (feedback, origin, continuity, focus, spatial change); stillness is the default.
output:
Ranked findings (most severe first):
1. [MAJOR] hero section - The hero carries three visually identical primary CTAs ('Start free trial', 'Book a demo', 'Watch the film'), each 160x48px in the same filled blue. With equal weight, size, and color, no single action reads as primary; a first-time visitor must deliberate instead of act. Principle: One primary action per screen; competing primaries force the user to do the designer's job [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#2, 1s-refactoring-ui#7]. Suggested fix: Keep one primary ('Start free trial') as the filled button; demote 'Book a demo' to a quiet secondary and 'Watch the film' to a text link. If two actions genuinely compete, the view is doing two jobs and should be split. (proposed, not applied)
2. [MAJOR] hero section - White 56px headline type is set over an unmuted looping video with only a partial 40% scrim; the subhead's final lines sit over bright footage and drop to roughly 2:1 effective contrast in those spots. Atmosphere is taxing legibility. Principle: Clarity: controls and text must be unmistakable; legibility beats atmosphere; the grayscale test [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#1, 1s-refactoring-ui#5, 1s-apple-hig#11]. Suggested fix: Either commit to a full-bleed scrim (60-70% gradient across the whole text block) or replace the video with a still frame dimmed to a consistent tone. Then re-check contrast line by line, not just at the headline. (proposed, not applied)
3. [MINOR] hero section - The 44-word subhead runs at 13px across a 640px measure, yielding ~105-115 characters per line. That is roughly double a comfortable reading measure at a size that already strains. Principle: Line length and body size serve the reader's eye; long lines make the return trip tiring [chunks: 1s-practical-typography#3, 1s-material-3#5]. Suggested fix: Reset the subhead to 17-18px, cap the measure near 560px (about 60-70 characters), and cut the copy to under 25 words. One idea, one breath. (proposed, not applied)
4. [MINOR] hero section - The 56px headline inherits body spacing (1.6 line-height, default tracking), so its two lines drift apart and read as disconnected large letters rather than one confident statement. Principle: Display type needs tighter spacing than body; judge headlines as shapes at their actual size [chunks: 1s-practical-typography#6]. Suggested fix: Set display type by eye at its actual size: tighten line-height toward 1.05-1.15 and apply slight negative tracking until the headline reads as a single shape. (proposed, not applied)
5. [MINOR] hero section - A 12-second looping video autoplays behind the hero with no pause control and no reduced-motion alternative. The motion explains nothing about the product or the user's position; it is decoration with a bandwidth cost. Principle: Every animation must explain something (feedback, origin, continuity, focus, spatial change); stillness is the default [chunks: 1s-emil-kowalski#1, 1s-emil-kowalski#2]. Suggested fix: Default to a still frame; play motion only on user request. Honor the OS reduced-motion setting with an instant static frame, and never make the value proposition depend on a moving background. (proposed, not applied)

[MAJOR] Three equally loud buttons is a hierarchy failure before it is a copy problem: the eye has no primary to land on, so the visitor must read and compare all three before knowing which is safe. The partial scrim means legibility varies line by line, and the screen fails the grayscale test: strip color and the subhead dissolves into the footage. Principle at stake: Clarity: controls and text must be unmistakable; legibility beats atmosphere; the grayscale test.

Step 2 - Typography. [MINOR] 13px is below the comfortable body floor for desktop marketing copy, and 105+ character lines force a long, error-prone eye return on every line. The type is asking the reader to work before the product has earned any attention. Principle at stake: Line length and body size serve the reader's eye; long lines make the return trip tiring. [MINOR] Body spacing applied to display type makes the headline read as scattered large letters instead of one visual unit; at 56px the whitespace inside and between letters dominates. brief.objective: Expert design critique of the navigation bar on the marketing site header for legal services firm. Rank findings by severity; every finding must name the region, the specific observable defect, and the principle violated.
brief.constraints:
Region under review: navigation bar (marketing site header, desktop web (1440px)).
The site header of a small-business legal services firm: left-aligned logo, a horizontal nav row, a search icon, and a right-side CTA on desktop web (1440px).
Observed: The nav row carries 11 top-level items: Products, Solutions, Pricing, Resources, Blog, Docs, Community, Customers, About, Careers, Contact. Each is 14px, equal weight, no grouping.
Observed: Nav links are 14px text with 28px row height and 8px horizontal padding, giving effective tap targets of roughly 28x40px on touch devices.
Observed: The 'Get started' CTA is a 13px text link in the same gray as the other nav items, sitting last after 'Contact'. Nothing in the header is visually louder than anything else.
Observed: The search and account icons are 24px with 2.5px strokes beside 14px regular nav text; the icons visibly dominate the labels.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the navigation bar of a small-business legal services firm (marketing site header) for founders seeking counsel on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] Eleven undifferentiated choices is a decision-tax at the top of every page. Comparison is cognitively expensive; the nav is asking visitors to do taxonomy work before they know what the company does. Principle at stake: Decision time grows with options; structure choices, group, and disclose progressively. [MINOR] When everything is quiet, nothing is. The single most important action on the site is styled exactly like the least important link, so the emphasis that should guide the eye is spent nowhere. Principle at stake: Contrast stands out only when rare: give the single most important action the emphasis.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MAJOR] 28px-tall targets are an error factory on touch: neighbors get hit by accident, and the miss cost is a wrong page load. Small targets are a mechanical failure, not a style choice. Principle at stake: Touch targets should be comfortably tappable, around 44pt, with spacing against mis-taps. [COSMETIC] Heavy icons next to light text break the partnership: the eye lands on the icon before the word it accompanies, so the nav reads as a row of symbols with footnotes. Principle at stake: Icons must match the text weight and optical size; the pair should read as one unit.
output:
Ranked findings (most severe first):
1. [MAJOR] navigation bar - The nav exposes 11 equal-weight top-level items with no grouping or progressive disclosure. Visitors must scan and compare eleven options on every page load before reaching content. Principle: Decision time grows with options; structure choices, group, and disclose progressively [chunks: 1s-laws-of-ux#3, 1s-nng#8]. Suggested fix: Cut to 4-6 primary items; fold the rest into grouped dropdowns (Product, Resources, Company). The nav's job is orientation, not sitemap. (proposed, not applied)
2. [MAJOR] navigation bar - Nav tap targets measure roughly 28x40px, well under the ~44pt comfortable minimum, with 8px gaps between adjacent links. Mis-taps are structurally likely. Principle: Touch targets should be comfortably tappable, around 44pt, with spacing against mis-taps [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#10]. Suggested fix: Raise the header row to 56-64px and give each link a full-height target with at least 12px separation. Keep the 14px label; enlarge the hit area, not the text. (proposed, not applied)
3. [MINOR] navigation bar - The 'Get started' CTA is set as 13px gray text identical to the other eleven links. The page's primary conversion action carries zero visual distinction. Principle: Contrast stands out only when rare: give the single most important action the emphasis [chunks: 1s-laws-of-ux#6]. Suggested fix: Give the CTA the one loud treatment in the header: filled button, brand color, adequate padding. Let everything else recede; boldness works only when it is rare. (proposed, not applied)
4. [COSMETIC] navigation bar - The 24px / 2.5px-stroke icons outweigh the 14px regular labels beside them; at a glance the icons draw the eye first and the text reads as secondary. Principle: Icons must match the text weight and optical size; the pair should read as one unit [chunks: 1s-refactoring-ui#11]. Suggested fix: Drop the icons to 20px with ~1.75px strokes to match the 14px regular text, and check the pair at a glance: neither element should win. (proposed, not applied)

brief.objective: Expert design critique of the pricing table on the pricing page for local HVAC company. Rank findings by severity; every finding must name the region, the specific observable defect, and the principle violated.

Observed: Each of the four plan columns uses its own accent hue (blue, green, purple, orange), plus a fifth red for the 'limited offer' ribbon: five hues carrying meaning on one screen.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the pricing table of a local heating-and-cooling business site (pricing page) for homeowners requesting quotes on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] Comparison is cognitively expensive, and this grid maximizes the cost: four columns times 34 rows with near-identical siblings. The visitor's decision is 'which of these near-twins', the hardest kind. Principle at stake: Simplify the decision: three clearly differentiated plans beat a scattered comparison grid. [MAJOR] Blur the screen and the prices disappear while the checkmarks march on: the hierarchy is built from content the visitor must read, not from design. On a pricing page the price is the headline and it is currently the quietest element. Principle at stake: Build hierarchy from weight, contrast, and spacing before size; the squint test. [STRENGTH] Proof placed at the decision point answers price hesitation with value proof, exactly where doubt spikes. One well-placed proof point outperforms the logo wall further down the page. Principle at stake: Social proof persuades at the moment of hesitation: placement, not volume.

Step 2 - Typography. [MINOR] At ~2.9:1 this fails even large-text thresholds and is functionally invisible to aging eyes and cheap screens. Footnotes carry the pricing terms; hiding them in gray reads as evasive whether intended or not. Principle at stake: Contrast is non-negotiable for text; decorative low-contrast text is the first thing to fail.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MINOR] Red-plus-strikethrough is a convention, but color-only encoding fails for color-blind users and for anyone scanning fast: the anchor reads as an error, not as a saving. A meaningful share of users cannot distinguish the signal. Principle at stake: Never rely on color alone to carry meaning; pair color with text or icon. [MINOR] Five accents teach the visitor that color means nothing in particular, which destroys the one place color should work: the recommended plan and its CTA. Restraint reads as confidence; this reads as decoration. Principle at stake: One accent color used consistently; more hues carrying meaning is noise, not personality.
output:
Ranked findings (most severe first):
1. [MAJOR] pricing table - Four plans across 34 feature rows with no recommended marker; the two middle tiers differ by one feature. The grid presents maximum comparison cost with minimum differentiation. Principle: Simplify the decision: three clearly differentiated plans beat a scattered comparison grid [chunks: 1s-laws-of-ux#3]. Suggested fix: Collapse to three tiers with real differentiation, mark one 'Most popular', and move the full 34-row matrix behind a 'Compare all features' disclosure. Structure the decision instead of displaying it. (proposed, not applied)
2. [MAJOR] pricing table - Prices at 20px regular gray sit beneath 16px near-black checkmark rows; in a squint test the prices vanish first. The page's most decision-relevant number is its least prominent element. Principle: Build hierarchy from weight, contrast, and spacing before size; the squint test [chunks: 1s-refactoring-ui#4]. Suggested fix: Promote prices to 32-36px semibold near-black with tight spacing above the CTA; quiet the feature rows to 14px gray. The eye should find the price in under a second, blurred or not. (proposed, not applied)
3. [MINOR] pricing table - The 'was' price is a red strikethrough with no accompanying label, so the discount meaning is encoded in color alone. Principle: Never rely on color alone to carry meaning; pair color with text or icon [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#10, 1s-ibm-carbon#10]. Suggested fix: Add an explicit 'Save 20%' label or 'billed annually' caption next to the anchor; keep the strikethrough as reinforcement, not as the only signal. (proposed, not applied)
4. [MINOR] pricing table - Legal footnotes at 10px #9a9a9a on white measure roughly 2.9:1 contrast, below every text threshold. The terms that govern the price are the least legible words on the page. Principle: Contrast is non-negotiable for text; decorative low-contrast text is the first thing to fail [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#10]. Suggested fix: Raise footnotes to 12px #595959 or darker (4.5:1+). Small text needs more contrast, not less. (proposed, not applied)
5. [MINOR] pricing table - Five distinct hues (blue, green, purple, orange, red) each carry meaning across the four plan columns. No single color is learnable as 'the action color'. Principle: One accent color used consistently; more hues carrying meaning is noise, not personality [chunks: 1s-refactoring-ui#10]. Suggested fix: Consolidate to one accent for the recommended plan and its CTA; render the other tiers in neutrals. Personality comes from one confident choice, not five competing ones. (proposed, not applied)
What works (confirmed with principle):

brief.objective: Expert design critique of the checkout form on the checkout flow for pet care subscription. Rank findings by severity; every finding must name the region, the specific observable defect, and the principle violated.
brief.constraints:
Region under review: checkout form (checkout flow, desktop web (1440px)).
The checkout of a pet-care subscription service on desktop web (1440px): a single long page collecting contact, shipping, billing, and payment details before any order summary.
Observed: The first checkout step requires creating an account: email, password, and password confirmation must be submitted before the shipping form appears. No guest path exists.
Observed: All 22 fields appear on one page: contact (3), shipping (8), billing (7), plus 'how did you hear about us', company name, and order notes. The form is roughly four viewports tall.
Observed: Submitting with an invalid card expiry shows a top-of-page banner reading 'Invalid input' and clears all 22 fields, including the valid ones. No field-level message appears.
Observed: All 22 fields use placeholder text as the only label; the placeholder vanishes on focus, leaving filled fields unlabeled.
Observed: Clicking 'Place order' shows a full-page spinner with no label for 3-5 seconds while payment processes. No skeleton, no progress, no confirmation of what is happening.
Observed: The flow shows 'Step 2 of 3: Shipping' at the top, each completed field gets a subtle checkmark, and the order total stays visible in a sticky summary.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the checkout form of a pet-care subscription service (checkout flow) for pet owners managing deliveries on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [CATASTROPHIC] The shopper's intent is to buy, not to join. Forcing account creation before payment converts a purchase into a membership decision and abandons the shoppers who refuse the trade. This is a catastrophic-severity gate on the core task. Principle at stake: Forced account creation is a classic wall; guest checkout should be the default. [MAJOR] Shoppers judge effort in the first seconds; a four-viewport wall reads as a chore before a single field is touched. Every unnecessary field is a unit of perceived workload and a potential validation failure. Principle at stake: Abandonment follows perceived workload: chunk fields into short steps rather than one sprawling form.

Step 2 - Typography. [MINOR] Placeholders-as-labels impose a memory tax: once typing starts, the shopper must remember what the field was. Cover the screen and ask what each filled field holds; whatever must be recalled is a finding. Principle at stake: Show options and labels in context; never demand memory or hide the label inside the field.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MAJOR] 'Invalid input' names no cause and no remedy, and wiping 21 correct fields punishes the shopper for one mistake. This is hostility wearing the costume of validation: the design scolds instead of guiding. Principle at stake: Errors must name the problem at the field in plain language and never destroy correct entries. [STRENGTH] Step indicators plus a visible finish line exploit the goal-gradient effect honestly: the shopper sees the end approaching and persists. Inline checkmarks reassure at the stressful moment instead of waiting for failure. Principle at stake: Visible progress converts amorphous effort into a race with a finish line; confirm correct input.

Step 4 - Motion. [MINOR] A silent frozen screen past the instantaneity threshold makes attention wander and invites double-submits. The system is working but telling nobody, which reads as broken. Principle at stake: Acknowledge waits immediately; an acknowledged wait feels shorter than a silent one.
output:
Ranked findings (most severe first):
1. [CATASTROPHIC] checkout form - Account creation (email + password + confirmation) is mandatory before the shipping form; there is no guest checkout. First-time shoppers cannot pay without joining. Principle: Forced account creation is a classic wall; guest checkout should be the default [chunks: 1s-baymard#7]. Suggested fix: Make guest checkout the default and most prominent path. Offer account creation after purchase, pre-filled, asking at most for a password. Sell the account when the conversion is already won. (proposed, not applied)
2. [MAJOR] checkout form - 22 fields on a single page, including non-fulfillment fields ('how did you hear about us', company, order notes). The visible workload is the abandonment driver, not the step count. Principle: Abandonment follows perceived workload: chunk fields into short steps rather than one sprawling form [chunks: 1s-baymard#0, 1s-baymard#3]. Suggested fix: Split into three short steps with a progress indicator; delete every field not required to fulfill the order; merge first/last name into 'full name'. Make each moment feel light. (proposed, not applied)
3. [MAJOR] checkout form - A single expiry error triggers a generic 'Invalid input' banner and erases all entered data; no field is marked, no fix is described. Correct effort is destroyed. Principle: Errors must name the problem at the field in plain language and never destroy correct entries [chunks: 1s-baymard#6, 1s-nng#9]. Suggested fix: Validate inline as each field completes; on error, mark the field, explain the fix ('Enter the 3-digit code on the back of your card'), and preserve every correct entry. Confirm valid input positively as the shopper goes. (proposed, not applied)
4. [MINOR] checkout form - Every field's label exists only as placeholder text that disappears on focus. Filled fields carry no visible label, forcing the shopper to hold 22 mappings in memory. Principle: Show options and labels in context; never demand memory or hide the label inside the field [chunks: 1s-nng#7]. Suggested fix: Use persistent floating or above-field labels; keep placeholders for examples ('MM / YY'), not for names. Instructions live where the action happens. (proposed, not applied)
5. [MINOR] checkout form - Order submission shows an unlabeled full-page spinner for 3-5 seconds. A distracted shopper cannot tell whether the payment is processing or the page died. Principle: Acknowledge waits immediately; an acknowledged wait feels shorter than a silent one [chunks: 1s-laws-of-ux#13, 1s-nng#2]. Suggested fix: Acknowledge immediately: keep the button in a loading state with 'Processing payment...', disable double-submit, and show what happens next. Never leave a frozen screen wondering. (proposed, not applied)
What works (confirmed with principle):
- CONFIRM: 'Step 2 of 3' framing with inline positive validation and a persistent total makes the workload feel finite and the shopper's progress real. Progress shown, not hidden. Why it works: Visible progress converts amorphous effort into a race with a finish line; confirm correct input [chunks: 1s-laws-of-ux#9, 1s-baymard#6].

reasoning_trace:

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [CATASTROPHIC] The shopper did mental math two screens ago; every new number now feels like a trick, and trust collapses exactly where card details are entered. Surprise costs are the top abandonment driver for a reason. Principle at stake: Total cost must be visible before the final commitment; late numbers feel like tricks. [MINOR] An empty promo box at the payment step manufactures hesitation: shoppers leave to hunt for codes, often landing on competitor or coupon sites, mid-purchase. The field serves a minority and taxes everyone. Principle at stake: Optional inputs belong behind disclosure; an empty promo box sends shoppers code-hunting.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MAJOR] Doubt peaks where card details are entered. Reassurance buried in the footer or on a separate security page does not count; if the shopper has to go find it, it is absent at the only moment it matters. Principle at stake: Trust signals work only at the moment of doubt: badges and guarantees belong near the card fields. [MINOR] On a phone, typing is painful and every mode-switch is friction at the highest-anxiety step. The system knows these fields are numeric and refuses to act on it. Principle at stake: Trigger the right keyboard per field; wrong keyboards are a leading mobile frustration.

Suggested fix: Show shipping and fees on the product page and in the cart; break down the total (subtotal, shipping, taxes, discounts) at every step. No number at payment should be a first sighting. Principle: Trust signals work only at the moment of doubt: badges and guarantees belong near the card fields [chunks: 1s-baymard#8]. brief.objective: Expert design critique of the display ad on the display ad unit for travel booking service. Rank findings by severity; every finding must name the region, the specific observable defect, and the principle violated.
brief.constraints:
Region under review: display ad (display ad unit, display unit (300x250)).
A 300x250 display ad for a boutique travel booking service: brand mark, headline, product shot, price, disclaimer, and CTA.
Observed: The brand logo occupies the top 90px at full color; the 8-word headline is 24px regular gray; the product shot fills the middle; the CTA is a 120x32px quiet button.
Observed: The offer disclaimer ('*with qualifying purchase, see site for details') is 7px #b0b0b0 on white, roughly 1.8:1 contrast.
Observed: The CTA button is the same teal as the product illustration's background wash; in grayscale the button disappears into the artwork.
Observed: The HTML5 unit loops 6 seconds across 5 frames; the CTA appears only in frame 4 (visible ~1.2s per loop), and the unit ignores the OS reduced-motion setting.
Observed: The unit also shows one 5-word headline, one product shot, one price, one CTA. No badge, no starburst, no secondary message.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the display ad of a boutique travel booking service (display ad unit) for travelers comparing itineraries on display unit (300x250). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] The loudest elements are the logo and the product photo; the headline, which carries the selling idea, is the quietest text on the unit. Hierarchy by decoration: the brand shouts, the message whispers. Principle at stake: Build hierarchy from weight and contrast before size; the message must survive the squint test. [STRENGTH] A 300x250 unit can carry exactly one idea; this one spends every pixel on it. With no competing elements, the single CTA inherits all the emphasis the layout can give. Principle at stake: One idea per screen; restraint over decoration.

Step 2 - Typography. [MAJOR] At 7px and ~1.8:1 this is not fine print, it is gray texture. Terms the buyer relies on must be legible; hiding them in sub-threshold type is a disclosure failure wearing a design choice. Principle at stake: Text that cannot be read is not disclosure; contrast and size minimums apply to the small print too.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MINOR] A CTA that relies on hue to separate from its background fails the moment color is removed or muted. The action must stand out through weight, contrast, and spacing first, with color as reinforcement. Principle at stake: Color is the weakest hierarchy tool; the primary action must survive the grayscale test.

Step 4 - Motion. [MAJOR] The call to action, the one element that must be findable, is visible one-fifth of the time. The motion explains nothing (no feedback, no continuity, no focus guidance); it rations the action. And vestibular-sensitive users get no relief. Principle at stake: Motion must explain something; honor reduced motion; never hide critical information mid-animation.
output:
Ranked findings (most severe first):
1. [MAJOR] display ad - In a 300x250 unit, the logo takes the top 90px while the 8-word headline sits at 24px regular gray. The selling message is visually subordinate to the brand mark. Principle: Build hierarchy from weight and contrast before size; the message must survive the squint test [chunks: 1s-refactoring-ui#4]. Suggested fix: Invert the emphasis: headline at 30-34px semibold near-black as the dominant element, logo at half its current size. In 300x250, every pixel must sell or leave. (proposed, not applied)
2. [MAJOR] display ad - The 7px #b0b0b0 disclaimer on white measures about 1.8:1 contrast: illegible on most screens, invisible on many. Principle: Text that cannot be read is not disclosure; contrast and size minimums apply to the small print too [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#10]. Suggested fix: Set disclaimers to at least 9-10px with 4.5:1 contrast, or shorten the claim so the disclaimer is unnecessary. Legibility is not optional for terms. (proposed, not applied)
3. [MAJOR] display ad - The CTA is visible only ~1.2s of each 6s loop (frame 4 of 5), and the unit does not honor reduced-motion preferences. The action is intermittently absent by design. Principle: Motion must explain something; honor reduced motion; never hide critical information mid-animation [chunks: 1s-emil-kowalski#1, 1s-emil-kowalski#8]. Suggested fix: Keep the CTA persistent across all frames; use motion only to draw the eye toward it, never to hide it. Provide a static end-frame for reduced-motion users. (proposed, not applied)
4. [MINOR] display ad - The teal CTA sits on a teal illustration wash; converted to grayscale, the button is indistinguishable from the background. The click target is camouflaged. Principle: Color is the weakest hierarchy tool; the primary action must survive the grayscale test [chunks: 1s-refactoring-ui#5]. Suggested fix: Give the CTA a high-contrast treatment independent of hue: near-black or white button with strong tonal separation from the artwork, then re-check in grayscale. (proposed, not applied)
What works (confirmed with principle):
- CONFIRM: 5-word headline, one product shot, one price, one CTA. The unit's entire visual budget funds a single message, and the action is unmissable. Why it works: One idea per screen; restraint over decoration [chunks: 1s-laws-of-ux#6, 1s-apple-hig#1].

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the dashboard stat card of a clinic appointment portal (analytics dashboard) for patients booking visits on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] Six equal metrics is six headlines: the eye has nowhere to land, so the card reports everything and prioritizes nothing. Squint and the grid is uniform noise; hierarchy must come from design, not from reading. Principle at stake: One dominant headline per screen; build hierarchy from weight, contrast, spacing before size. [STRENGTH] The display role does exactly its job: the major number is unmistakable, weight (not color) carries the emphasis, and the delta is readable as words. Typography disciplined, hierarchy instant. Principle at stake: Display roles exist for hero moments and major numbers; weight carries meaning.

Step 2 - Typography. [MINOR] Six orphan styles on a single card means the type scale is being invented per element. 'They all looked fine' is how interfaces quietly become incoherent. Principle at stake: Every string maps to a type role; orphan styles signal hierarchy solved with typography instead of layout.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MINOR] Color-only deltas fail color-blind users and mislead everyone else when 'down' is good: the encoding carries two meanings (direction, judgment) in one hue. Charts are components with the same contracts as buttons. Principle at stake: Never encode meaning in color alone; pair it with labels or icons.

Step 4 - Motion. [MINOR] A dashboard is opened dozens of times a day: a 2s flourish on each load is the inverted budget, lavish motion on the routine path. The animation delays the very reading it decorates. Principle at stake: Frequency governs the motion budget: high-frequency views must be near-instant.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the data table of a local heating-and-cooling business site (admin data table) for homeowners requesting quotes on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MINOR] Icon-only row actions demand recall instead of recognition, and parking delete 4px from edit with no confirmation turns a slip into data loss. Recognition over memory, and distance for danger. Principle at stake: Controls must be unmistakable; labels beat hidden commands; never require experimentation.

Step 2 - Typography. [MINOR] Proportional numerals in a data column destroy scannability: the eye cannot compare magnitudes down a ragged edge. Inconsistency is the typographic equivalent of a shaky voice. Principle at stake: Invisible consistency signals competence: tabular numerals, aligned columns, same treatment everywhere.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MINOR] Full cell borders plus zebra plus hover is visual noise cubed: every border competes for attention and none means anything. The amateur signature is a box around everything. Principle at stake: Borders must solve a structural problem or not exist; delete all borders and add back only the needed ones. [COSMETIC] Thirteen grays that are 'close enough' is the palette failing quietly: no gray has a learnable meaning, and hover vs selected vs disabled blur together. Roles, not samples. Principle at stake: Assign semantic color roles from tonal ramps; ad-hoc grays are a palette failure. [STRENGTH] Density as a switch beats a one-size answer: the power user gets throughput, the newcomer gets breathing room, and the same component tree serves both. The right complexity in the right place. Principle at stake: Density is a user-level variable: serve the power user and the newcomer from the same tree.

Ranked findings (most severe first):
1. [MINOR] data table - 1px borders on all four sides of every cell, combined with zebra rows and hover fills. Three redundant separation systems on one table. Principle: Borders must solve a structural problem or not exist; delete all borders and add back only the needed ones [chunks: 1s-refactoring-ui#8]. Suggested fix: Delete all cell borders; keep horizontal row dividers (or zebra spacing) only. Most tables keep fewer than half their borders after the audit. (proposed, not applied)
2. [MINOR] data table - 12px proportional numerals in amount columns with centered headers over left-aligned cells. Values cannot be scanned or compared down the column. Principle: Invisible consistency signals competence: tabular numerals, aligned columns, same treatment everywhere [chunks: 1s-practical-typography#9]. Suggested fix: Set numeric columns in tabular figures, right-align amounts, left-align headers to match. Decide the rule once, apply it without exception. (proposed, not applied)
3. [MINOR] data table - 4 unlabeled 16px icon actions per row, no tooltips; delete sits 4px from edit. Users must memorize meanings and cannot afford a slip. Principle: Controls must be unmistakable; labels beat hidden commands; never require experimentation [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#9, 1s-nng#7]. Suggested fix: Label the actions (text or tooltip at minimum), give delete a confirmation, and separate destructive actions from common ones. If a first-time user must guess, the control failed. (proposed, not applied)
4. [COSMETIC] data table - 13 near-identical grays with no role mapping; hover, selected, and disabled states are visually ambiguous. Principle: Assign semantic color roles from tonal ramps; ad-hoc grays are a palette failure [chunks: 1s-material-3#2, 1s-material-3#1]. Suggested fix: Define 4-5 semantic surface/text roles from one neutral ramp (surface, container-low/high, on-surface, on-surface-variant) and map every usage to a role. Delete the rest. (proposed, not applied)

- CONFIRM: a user-level density toggle (48px/32px rows) lets the table serve scanning and reading without forking the component. Density as a variable, not a constant. Why it works: Density is a user-level variable: serve the power user and the newcomer from the same tree [chunks: 1s-ibm-carbon#9].

reasoning_trace:

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] Three equally loud buttons in a 720px dialog force the user to read all three before knowing which is safe, exactly the failure the one-primary rule exists to prevent. When two actions genuinely compete, the view is doing two jobs. Principle at stake: One primary action per screen, visually louder than everything around it.

Depth answers 'where am I'; here the answer is ambiguous, and clicks leak through to the page behind. Principle at stake: Layers have meaning: modals sit above the flow; dim what is beneath so attention moves. [MINOR] Focus escaping to a dimmed (or undimmed) page behind the dialog is a keyboard trap in reverse: screen-reader and keyboard users lose their place entirely. These are the awkward states that must be defined, not discovered. Principle at stake: Keyboard contracts are component-level: dialogs trap focus, and every state has a defined behavior.

Step 4 - Motion. [MINOR] Symmetric 400ms timing treats appearing and leaving as the same job. They are not: entrances orient, exits obey. A lingering exit feels like the interface is slow to obey a decision already made. Principle at stake: Exits should be faster than entrances; symmetric timing means nobody thought about direction.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the filter sidebar of an online course marketplace (product listing page) for career-switchers comparing courses on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] Two hundred visible checkboxes is the decision cost maximized: the shopper must scan an inventory to buy one item. Progressive disclosure exists for exactly this shape of problem. Principle at stake: Structure choices: group, chunk, disclose progressively, preselect defaults.

Step 2 - Typography. [MINOR] When labels and options share size, weight, and color, grouping must be read, not seen; the 8px gaps are too tight to do the work either. Hierarchy built from content, not design. Principle at stake: Hierarchy from weight, contrast, spacing; group labels must outrank options.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MINOR] Users mis-filter constantly; the escape hatch is a whisper at the bottom of a very tall panel. If leaving costs effort, people abandon instead of correcting. Principle at stake: Every reachable state needs a clearly marked way back; retreat must be cheap.
output:
Ranked findings (most severe first):
1. [MAJOR] filter sidebar - 14 expanded groups, 200+ visible checkboxes, 47 brands with no in-group search. The filter panel is a second catalog. Principle: Structure choices: group, chunk, disclose progressively, preselect defaults [chunks: 1s-laws-of-ux#3]. Suggested fix: Show the top 5-6 options per group with 'Show more' disclosure; add search inside long groups; collapse low-use groups by default. Chunk the decision visibly. (proposed, not applied)

Principle: Every reachable state needs a clearly marked way back; retreat must be cheap [chunks: 1s-nng#4]. Suggested fix: Pin a visible 'Clear all (n)' control at the top of the panel whenever filters are active, and show applied filters as removable chips. The way back should be the easiest path. (proposed, not applied)

Principle: Hierarchy from weight, contrast, spacing; group labels must outrank options [chunks: 1s-refactoring-ui#4]. reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the mobile tab bar of a consumer budgeting app (mobile app tab bar) for young adults managing spending on iOS app (390px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] Seven destinations in a tab bar exceeds the platform pattern (4-5) and the labels are unreadably small; novelty here is a cost charged to every session. A tab bar that needs a manual is not a tab bar. Principle at stake: Decision time grows with options; platform patterns earn their keep by being standard.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MAJOR] 36px targets with 2px gaps on the highest-frequency control in the app is an error factory at thumb scale. Small targets are a mechanical failure, and here they guard every screen in the product. Principle at stake: Interactive elements should be comfortably tappable, around 44pt, with spacing against mis-taps. [STRENGTH] Tonal container plus filled-vs-outline icon is a selected state unmistakable from any other state: the state machine is visible and systematic. Consistency here is what makes an interface feel solid. Principle at stake: Selected states must be distinct from hover; state layers make feedback identical across components.

Step 4 - Motion. [MINOR] Tab switching is among the highest-frequency interactions in any app; 350ms of theater per switch, queued when tapped fast, is the inverted budget made visible. A minute a day lost to waiting. Principle at stake: High-frequency interactions must be near-instant; tab switches happen hundreds of times a day.

Suggested fix: Cut to 4-5 destinations; move the rest into a 'More' tab or contextual navigation. Use the platform pattern first; customize only with justification. (proposed, not applied)

Region under review: settings page (account settings page, desktop web (1440px)).
The account settings page of a nonprofit fundraising site's product on desktop web (1440px): preferences, notifications, and workspace controls.
Observed: 40 toggles and selects run in one unbroken column with 12px gaps; notification, privacy, billing, and workspace controls interleave with no headings.
Observed: A red 'Delete workspace' button sits 16px below the blue 'Save changes' button, same size (160x44px), in the same button row.
Observed: Toggling settings gives no indication of unsaved changes; navigating away silently discards edits with no warning.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the settings page of a nonprofit fundraising site (account settings page) for donors deciding to give on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MAJOR] Forty undifferentiated controls with uniform spacing says nothing about structure; the user must read every label to understand the page's grammar. When everything is evenly spaced, spacing says nothing. Principle at stake: Proximity is grammar: place related fields in one card, separate sections with whitespace.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MAJOR] Delete-as-neighbor-to-save is the catastrophic adjacency: one slip, one mis-tap, and the destructive action fires from the most common path on the page. Distance is the cheapest safety device. Principle at stake: Destructive actions are visually distant from the primary; keep them smaller and farther from common paths. [MINOR] The interface keeps the user uninformed about the single most important state on the page: whether their work is saved. Silence here manufactures data loss. Principle at stake: Every action should produce feedback; silence about state is the enemy.
output:
Ranked findings (most severe first):
1. [MAJOR] settings page - 40 controls in a single 12px-gap column, four domains interleaved, no headings. The page's structure must be read; it cannot be seen. Principle: Proximity is grammar: place related fields in one card, separate sections with whitespace [chunks: 1s-laws-of-ux#5]. Suggested fix: Group into labeled sections (Notifications, Privacy, Billing, Workspace) with 32px section gaps and 16px within; consider tabs if sections grow. Let proximity do the organizing. (proposed, not applied)
2. [MAJOR] settings page - 'Delete workspace' (160x44px red) sits 16px beneath 'Save changes' (160x44px blue). The irreversible action shares size, row, and reach with the routine one. Principle: Destructive actions are visually distant from the primary; keep them smaller and farther from common paths [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#2, 1s-laws-of-ux#2]. Suggested fix: Move destructive actions to a separated 'Danger zone' section at the page bottom with a confirmation step; never place them in the primary action row. (proposed, not applied)
3. [MINOR] settings page - No unsaved-changes indicator; leaving the page discards edits silently. The user cannot tell saved from unsaved. Principle: Every action should produce feedback; silence about state is the enemy [chunks: 1s-nng#2]. Suggested fix: Show a persistent 'Unsaved changes' indicator with Save/Discard, and warn on navigation with unsaved edits. A distracted user glancing at the screen should know the state. (proposed, not applied)

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the profile page of a fitness coaching app (user profile page) for new members starting programs on mobile web (390px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 1 - Hierarchy. [MINOR] On a phone viewport, 320px of cover is the stagehand's portrait where the actor should stand: the user's actual content starts where the screen ends. Deference means the chrome retreats. Principle at stake: Content is the hero; chrome gets out of the way; one path through each screen.

Step 2 - Typography. [COSMETIC] An unbroken 200-character block at tight spacing is a reading chore the user didn't choose: lines tangle, thoughts blur together. Paragraph treatment is how one thought ends and the next begins. Principle at stake: Line length and spacing keep lines from tangling; paragraphs need separation.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MINOR] A hidden progress meter cannot create a goal-gradient effect: the finish line is invisible, so the motivation it should manufacture never arrives. Showing a partially complete profile motivates; hiding it wastes the asset. Principle at stake: Visible progress energizes; hidden progress does not motivate; make the finish line visible.
output:

1. [MINOR] profile page - 320px cover photo on a 390px viewport; name, bio, and actions all fall below the fold. Decoration outranks content. Principle: Content is the hero; chrome gets out of the way; one path through each screen [chunks: 1s-apple-hig#3, 1s-apple-hig#8]. Suggested fix: Cap the cover at 120-140px on mobile; let the profile content own the first screen. Full-bleed content where it matters, chrome where it doesn't. (proposed, not applied)
2. [MINOR] profile page - 60%-complete meter buried in tab 3. The profile's best completion lever is invisible on the main view. Principle: Visible progress energizes; hidden progress does not motivate; make the finish line visible [chunks: 1s-laws-of-ux#9]. Suggested fix: Surface the meter on the profile header with the next missing item named ('Add a bio to reach 80%'). Visible distance remaining is the motivator. (proposed, not applied)
3. [COSMETIC] profile page - Bio renders as a single 200-char block, 14px/1.4, no breaks. The member's own words are hard to read. Principle: Line length and spacing keep lines from tangling; paragraphs need separation [chunks: 1s-practical-typography#3]. Suggested fix: Preserve the author's line breaks, set bio text at 15-16px with 1.6 line-height. Respect the content's own structure. (proposed, not applied)

brief.constraints:
Region under review: help tooltip (in-product help tooltip, desktop web (1440px)).
An in-product help tooltip in a growth-stage SaaS analytics product's app on desktop web (1440px): the small popup explaining a tricky control.
Observed: The tooltip is a 280px-wide paragraph of 68 words explaining the entire feature, covering the trigger button on hover.
Observed: The tooltip appears with 0ms delay on hover and flickers when the cursor crosses the 4px gap between trigger and popup; it vanishes instantly on mouse-out with no grace period.

reasoning_trace:
Context: critiquing the help tooltip of a growth-stage SaaS analytics product (in-product help tooltip) for product managers evaluating dashboards on desktop web (1440px). Audience and buying context set the severity lens for what follows.

Step 3 - Optical detail. [MINOR] A 68-word tooltip is documentation wearing a tooltip's clothes: it obscures the control it explains and demands a reading task for a glance's job. Short enough to actually be read is the bar. Principle at stake: Help at the point of confusion should be short enough to actually be read; tooltips are hints, not manuals.

Step 4 - Motion. [MINOR] Zero-delay hover plus a 4px dead gap makes the tooltip strobe: it appears before intent is clear and dies mid-read. Real interfaces are not videos; users act mid-animation, and hover needs a grace model. Principle at stake: Feedback should be visible without being noisy; hover intent needs a delay, and motion must be interruptible.

Suggested fix: Cut to 1-2 lines naming what the control does ('Exports the filtered view as CSV'); move the 68-word explanation to the linked docs page. Hints here, manuals there. (proposed, not applied)

Principle: Feedback should be visible without being noisy; hover intent needs a delay, and motion must be interruptible [chunks: 1s-nng#2, 1s-emil-kowalski#6].
